title: Right temporal headache and blurred vision in a 64-year-old man
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 64-year-old man in the ED with 16 hours of right temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and a blurred right eye. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, which show worsening vision while every vital sign stays in the white zone, and his blood results. They then manage giant cell arteritis with visual involvement as a sight-threatening emergency and explain the diagnosis, treatment and red flags to the patient.
focus: New headache over 50: recognising giant cell arteritis with visual involvement and starting high-dose corticosteroids without delay
stem: You are the junior medical officer in the Emergency Department of a major metropolitan hospital. Fred Harleman, a 64-year-old university lecturer, has come in with a headache. He is sitting on a trolley in a cubicle. A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Harleman and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Start any immediate management you think he needs as you go (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations and blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Fred Harleman, aged 64, an art history lecturer at a university. You are sitting up on the trolley and keep rubbing your right temple. You are articulate and polite, a little frustrated that you have to be here, and increasingly worried. Give the history below only when asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've had this headache since last night and it just won't go away. I'm really hoping it's just a migraine or something."

The headache (give only when asked)

  • Site: right-sided, centred on the right temple. It spreads a little to the back of the head.
  • Onset: it came on gradually. You first noticed it at about 9 o'clock last night while watching television. It got gradually worse from there.
  • Character: an ache. It is not sharp and not throbbing.
  • Time course: constant for about 16 hours. It has not gone away at all.
  • Severity: 6/10.
  • Aggravating and relieving factors: nothing makes it worse. You took Panadol at home and it made little difference.

Other symptoms (give only when asked about the scalp, chewing or vision)

  • Scalp: "I noticed that my scalp was sore when I was combing my hair today."
  • Jaw: "My jaw started to feel sore during breakfast and lunch today. It was mainly towards the end of my meal, but it felt better after I stopped eating." No toothache.
  • Vision: "My right eye has gone blurry." You noticed it this morning when reading the paper. It is only the right eye; the left eye is fine. It has been there since and has not come and gone. No double vision, no flashing lights, no pain in the eye, no red eye and no halos around lights. You have not had any brief blackouts of vision before today.

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • Shoulders and hips: no stiffness or aching in the shoulders, neck or hips, including first thing in the morning. You can lift your arms and get out of a chair without trouble.
  • No sudden "worst ever" headache; it did not come on like a thunderclap.
  • No fever or sweats, no neck stiffness, no discomfort with bright lights, no rash.
  • No nausea or vomiting. No aura or zigzag lines.
  • No weight loss, no loss of appetite, no night sweats, and no more tired than usual.
  • The headache is no worse in the mornings or on lying down, coughing or straining. No change in behaviour or memory (your wife would have told you). No weakness, numbness, slurred speech or trouble with balance.
  • No watering eye, runny or blocked nose, or drooping eyelid on the side of the pain.
  • No band-like tightness and no unusual stress.
  • You don't really get headaches, and you have never had one like this.
  • No head injury.
  • No diabetes, no stomach ulcers, no thinning of the bones that you know of, no recent infections and no TB.

Past medical history

  • High blood pressure.
  • Keyhole repair of hernias in both groins 5 years ago, with no problems.

Medications and allergies

  • Irbesartan 150 mg once a day.
  • A multivitamin.
  • No allergies.

Family history

  • Your mother died of a heart attack at 86.
  • Your father died of a stroke at 82.
  • Your brother Tom, 59, has high blood pressure.

Social history

  • You smoked a pack a day for 5 years and quit 10 years ago.
  • One to two glasses of red wine on weekends. No other drugs.
  • You lecture in art history at a university.
  • You walk 1 to 2 hours a week. You and your wife share the home cooking.
  • You live with your wife. You belong to an art appreciation society. Your son William lives 25 minutes away.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: "I'm really hoping it's just a migraine or something."
  • Concerns: "It's a bit frustrating that I have to be here, and my family are worried about me too." If the candidate explores further: "I'm starting to worry something serious could be going on."
  • Expectations: you would like something to fix the headache and to know what is going on.
  • Question to ask: "Is it something to do with my eye? Should I be worried about the blurriness?"

During the station

  • About halfway through, say: "Sorry, my right eye seems to be getting worse. It's like a smudge over the bottom half."

The nurse (played by the examiner)

  • Gives the observations and a bedside glucose when asked (see the Exam findings).
  • If the candidate orders a cannula, bloods, analgesia, corticosteroids or a referral, says "I'll get that started". If a drug is ordered without a dose or route, asks "What dose and route would you like?" If paracetamol is given, it makes little difference, as at home.
  • If the candidate asks for blood results, says they will be available in Part 2.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: alert and comfortable at rest, rubbing his right temple. Weight 82 kg.
  • Observations: RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 156/88, HR 86 regular, temperature 37.4 °C, pain 6/10, CRT 2 seconds. Bedside glucose 6.0 mmol/L.
  • Temporal arteries and scalp: the right superficial temporal artery is thickened, nodular and tender, and its pulse is barely palpable. The left temporal artery is soft with a normal pulse. The scalp is tender over the right temple and parietal area. No rash or vesicles. Sinuses not tender. Temporomandibular joints non-tender, teeth normal.
  • Visual acuity (with his glasses): right 6/18, no better with a pinhole; left 6/6. If acuity is re-checked after he reports worsening: right 6/36, left 6/6.
  • Pupils: equal at rest. Swinging light test: right relative afferent pupillary defect.
  • Colour vision (if tested): reduced in the right eye (misses several Ishihara plates), normal on the left.
  • Visual fields to confrontation: loss of the inferior field in the right eye; left full.
  • Fundoscopy: right optic disc is pale and swollen, with a small flame haemorrhage at the disc margin. Left disc normal. No papilloedema on the left.
  • Eyes: both eyes white and quiet, corneas clear, neither eye hard or tender.
  • Other cranial nerves: eye movements full with no double vision, no ptosis, face symmetrical, hearing, palate and tongue normal.
  • Meningism: no neck stiffness, Kernig's sign negative, no photophobia, no rash.
  • Limbs and gait: tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination normal and symmetrical. Plantars flexor. Gait normal.
  • Shoulders and hips: full active and passive range, no tenderness, no synovitis.
  • Cardiovascular: pulse 86 regular. BP right arm 156/88, left arm 152/86. Radial and brachial pulses equal. No carotid, subclavian or axillary bruits. Heart sounds dual, no murmur.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms the patient's identity and gains consent before examining.
Acknowledges his frustration and his family's worry with empathy, uses plain language and responds to his question about the blurred eye honestly.
History
Characterises the headache:

kids.x: Site and radiation: right temple, spreading a little to the back of the head
Onset and course: gradual, first noticed about 9 pm last night, constant for about 16 hours
Character and severity: an ache, not sharp or throbbing, 6/10
Nothing worsens it and Panadol had little effect

check.x: Asks specifically about the features of giant cell arteritis and elicits:

kids.x: Scalp tenderness when combing his hair
Jaw claudication: jaw pain towards the end of breakfast and lunch that settles when he stops eating
Blurred vision in the right eye

check.x: Characterises the visual symptom: one eye only, noticed this morning and persistent, no double vision, no earlier transient episodes, and no red or painful eye or halos.
Screens for polymyalgia rheumatica (shoulder, neck and hip stiffness, especially in the morning) and for constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats, fatigue).
Screens for dangerous secondary causes of headache:

kids.x: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: thunderclap or 'worst ever' onset
Meningitis: fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, rash
Intracranial mass: worse in the morning or on lying, coughing or straining, vomiting, weight loss, behaviour change, focal weakness

check.x: Screens for primary headaches: migraine (aura, nausea, photophobia, past similar headaches), cluster headache (eye watering, nasal symptoms, drooping eyelid) and tension-type headache (band-like pain, stress).
Takes the past history, medications and allergies:

kids.x: Hypertension and bilateral laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair 5 years ago
Irbesartan 150 mg daily and a multivitamin
No allergies

check.x: Asks about conditions that high-dose corticosteroids could worsen: diabetes, peptic ulcer, osteoporosis and current or past infection, including TB.
Takes a brief family and social history: vascular family history, ex-smoker about 5 pack-years, alcohol, lives with wife.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: hoping it is a migraine, frustrated about being here, family worried, and fearing something serious.
Examination
Asks for a full set of observations and a bedside glucose (BP 156/88, temperature 37.4 °C, otherwise normal; glucose 6.0 mmol/L).
Palpates both temporal arteries and the scalp and finds a thickened, nodular, tender right temporal artery with a barely palpable pulse, plus right scalp tenderness.
Examines the eyes and finds right optic nerve ischaemia:

kids.x: Visual acuity in each eye: right 6/18 (no better with a pinhole), left 6/6
Swinging light test: right relative afferent pupillary defect
Visual fields (right inferior field loss) or colour vision (reduced on the right)
Fundoscopy: pale, swollen right optic disc with a flame haemorrhage; left disc normal

check.x: Examines the other cranial nerves, including eye movements and ptosis, and the limbs, and finds no focal deficit.
Examines for meningism (neck stiffness, Kernig's sign, photophobia, rash) and finds none.
Examines the shoulder and hip girdles for polymyalgia, or screens for large-vessel involvement (BP in both arms, upper limb pulses, subclavian and axillary bruits).
Immediate management

Recognises that the visual loss (and the reported worsening) is a sight-threatening emergency. Before the end of Part 1, orders IV methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g with dose and route (after cannula and bloods including ESR and CRP), without waiting for results, and asks for a senior ED doctor and urgent ophthalmology.
check.d: Part 1 item. The nurse confirms the order; the first dose starts at 14:10.

check.x: Interpretation

Interprets the observations: every vital sign is in the white zone, but the right acuity falls from 6/18 to 6/36 with the nurse concerned. States that this needs immediate medical review (staff concern is itself a Clinical Review criterion) and that a white zone chart does not make him safe.
Interprets the ESR (86) and CRP (78) as markedly raised and supporting giant cell arteritis.

Interprets the rest of the bloods: thrombocytosis, mild normocytic anaemia, raised ALP and low albumin fit systemic inflammation. Normal glucose and renal function are the baseline before steroids. A normal white cell count argues against bacterial infection.

Gives giant cell arteritis with right arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy as the diagnosis. Supports it with age over 50, a new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss, an abnormal temporal artery and a raised ESR and CRP.

Names at least three differentials, each with a feature against it, from: non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, migraine, tension-type headache, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis and intracranial mass.
Management
Treats this as a sight-threatening emergency: brings a senior ED doctor to the bedside now and requests urgent ophthalmology review today.
Starts high-dose corticosteroids immediately:

kids.x: IV methylprednisolone (500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days) because the vision is affected
kids.d: Credit if ordered in Part 1 (item 23) or stated in Part 2.

kids.x: Followed by oral prednisolone 60 mg daily (about 1 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg), tapered slowly by rheumatology
States that steroids are not delayed for the biopsy or ultrasound, and are not stopped if the biopsy is negative while clinical suspicion remains high

check.x: Admits him under rheumatology, with ophthalmology co-managing.
Arranges confirmation: temporal artery biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks of starting steroids, or temporal artery ultrasound (ideally within the first week).
Plans for steroid adverse effects: blood glucose monitoring, BP, calcium and vitamin D with bone protection, a bone density assessment, and gastric protection where indicated.
Gives simple analgesia (regular paracetamol) and orders repeated visual acuity checks of both eyes.

Explains in plain words that this is not a migraine but inflammation of the arteries supplying the head and eye. Is honest that the right eye's vision may not recover and that treatment aims to protect both eyes. Explains the long steroid course and the biopsy.
Safety netting

Sets in-hospital escalation triggers: any further change in vision in either eye (especially the left), double vision, new stroke symptoms, or worsening headache or jaw pain. Tells Fred to report these to the nurse at once.

Tells Fred in plain words that after discharge any new blurring or loss of vision, double vision, or face or limb weakness or speech trouble means calling 000. Also tells him never to stop the steroids suddenly.
Arranges follow-up: rheumatology clinic and ophthalmology review, GP monitoring of ESR/CRP, glucose and BP, and no driving until his vision has been assessed.

part2.lead: It is now 14:45. Here are Fred's observations since he arrived and his blood results. If methylprednisolone was ordered in Part 1, the first dose started at 14:10.
part2.patient:
Fred is worried but calm. As the candidate explains, ask these once each:

  • "So it's not a migraine, then?"
  • "Will my eye get better?"
  • "How long will I be on these steroids?"

If the candidate uses jargon ("arteritis", "optic neuropathy", "biopsy"), ask "What does that mean?" If the candidate says he needs to stay in hospital, say: "Well, if it's my eyesight, I'd better stay."

handover.label: Observations since arrival
handover.result: Room air throughout. Visual acuity is measured with his glasses. Left eye 6/6 at every check.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 16 to 18, SpO2 96 to 97% on room air, BP 152 to 158 systolic, HR 84 to 90 regular, temperature 37.4 to 37.5 °C and alert. Every value is in the white zone at all three times. Pain stays at 6/10. Triage glucose is 6.0. From 14:00 the nurse is concerned: right acuity has fallen from 6/18 to 6/36 and the right eye is now 'like fog'. The left eye is unchanged at 6/6.
  • Meaning: ischaemic visual loss in the right eye is progressing over hours, and the vital signs do not show it. A low-grade temperature fits systemic inflammation, not sepsis. BP is mildly raised in a man with known hypertension and pain.
  • Changes: none of the numbers trigger a clinical review or rapid response. Under Between the Flags, nurse concern is itself a Clinical Review criterion, so escalation is mandated even with every value in the white zone. The nurse's concern and the worsening vision call for immediate medical review: senior ED doctor now, IV methylprednisolone now, or confirm the first dose is running, ophthalmology today, and acuity in both eyes checked regularly, with any change in the left eye escalated at once. The glucose is the baseline before steroids.

rows.note: Triage: headache and blurred right eye. VA right 6/18, left 6/6
Says right eye worse than on arrival. VA right 6/36, left 6/6
Right eye 'like looking through fog'. Left eye unchanged. Doctor informed

handover.label: Blood results
handover.model:
• Read: ESR 86 and CRP 78 are markedly raised. Platelets 512 (thrombocytosis). Hb 121 with a normal MCV (mild normocytic anaemia). WCC and neutrophils are normal. ALP is mildly raised at 138 with a normal ALT and bilirubin. Albumin is low at 33. Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine (eGFR 81) and random glucose 6.2 are normal.
  • Meaning: a strong acute phase response that fits giant cell arteritis. An ESR of 50 or more is a classification criterion, and thrombocytosis is linked with a higher risk of ischaemic visual loss. Anaemia of inflammation, a raised ALP and a low albumin are common in GCA. A normal WCC makes bacterial infection unlikely. A normal ESR would not have excluded GCA.
  • Changes: the results support steroids now but do not confirm the diagnosis, so biopsy or ultrasound is still needed. Normal glucose and renal function are the baseline for monitoring on high-dose steroids.

ask: You are now calling the rheumatology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Fred Harleman, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Fred now, here in the emergency department.
Fred asks you, "What is this, and will my eye get better?" Please answer him, including what he should watch out for and the follow-up he will need.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED JMO; Fred Harleman, 64.
  • Situation: suspected giant cell arteritis with worsening right eye vision in the ED; needs IV steroids and admission.
  • Background: 16 hours of right temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication; right eye blurred since this morning; no PMR symptoms; hypertension on irbesartan; no diabetes or ulcers; no allergies.
  • Assessment: obs all white zone but nurse concerned, BP 156/88, T 37.4; right acuity 6/18 falling to 6/36, right RAPD, pale swollen right disc; tender, thickened, pulseless right temporal artery; ESR 86, CRP 78, platelets 512, Hb 121.
  • Recommendation: IV methylprednisolone now (or first dose running since 14:10); ophthalmology today; please accept under rheumatology and arrange temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound.

Giant cell arteritis with right arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy: aged 64, new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, right visual loss with RAPD and a pale swollen disc, an abnormal right temporal artery, ESR 86 and CRP 78.

  • Non-arteritic AION: for: 64, hypertensive, altitudinal loss with disc swelling; against: pale rather than hyperaemic disc, headache, jaw claudication, abnormal temporal artery, ESR 86 and CRP 78.
  • Migraine: his own hope; against: new at 64, not throbbing, no nausea, photophobia or aura.
  • Tension-type headache: against: unilateral, scalp and jaw symptoms, visual loss.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: against: gradual onset, no thunderclap, no meningism.
  • Meningitis: against: no fever, neck stiffness, photophobia or rash; normal WCC.
  • Intracranial mass: against: no morning or postural headache, no weight loss or behaviour change, no papilloedema or focal signs.

1. Sight-threatening emergency: senior ED doctor to the bedside now.
  2. IV methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days, first dose now (or confirm it is running), without waiting for biopsy; then oral prednisolone 60 mg daily (about 1 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg), tapered slowly by rheumatology. Without visual involvement, oral prednisolone alone.
  3. Urgent ophthalmology review today.
  4. Admit under rheumatology.
  5. Temporal artery biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks of starting steroids, or ultrasound ideally within the first week; a negative biopsy does not stop treatment if suspicion stays high.
  6. Steroid care: glucose monitoring, BP, calcium and vitamin D with bone protection, bone density assessment, gastric protection if indicated.
  7. Regular paracetamol; repeat visual acuity in both eyes.
  8. Nurse escalation: any change in either eye, double vision, stroke symptoms.

• What it is: not a migraine; inflammation of the arteries of the head (giant cell arteritis) has cut the blood supply to the nerve at the back of the right eye.
  • The eye: honestly, vision already lost may not come back; treatment is urgent to stop it worsening and to protect the left eye.
  • Steroids: a drip for 3 days, then tablets reduced slowly over many months (often a year or more); never stop suddenly.
  • Biopsy: a small cut at the temple to confirm it.
  • Red flags: any new blurring or loss of vision in either eye, double vision, or face or limb weakness or speech trouble: tell the nurse now; after discharge call 000.
  • Follow-up: rheumatology, ophthalmology and GP; no driving until vision is assessed.

ddx.dx: Giant cell arteritis with right arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
ddx.for: A 64-year-old with a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, worsening right visual loss with RAPD and a pale swollen disc, a tender pulseless right temporal artery, ESR 86 and CRP 78.
ddx.against: He has no polymyalgia or constitutional symptoms, which are common but not required.

ddx.for: He is 64 and hypertensive, with painless altitudinal field loss and a swollen right disc.
ddx.against: The disc is pale (chalky) rather than hyperaemic, and he has headache, jaw claudication, an abnormal temporal artery and ESR 86 with CRP 78.

ddx.for: He has a unilateral headache and hopes it is a migraine.
ddx.against: It is new at 64 in a man who does not get headaches, it is an ache rather than throbbing, and he has no nausea, photophobia or aura.

ddx.for: The pain is a constant, non-throbbing ache.
ddx.against: It is one-sided, with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual loss, and he has no stress or band-like tightness.

ddx.for: He has a new headache at 64 with hypertension.
ddx.against: The onset was gradual, not thunderclap, and he has no meningism, vomiting or focal signs.

ddx.for: He has a new headache over 50 with a visual disturbance.
ddx.against: The headache is not worse in the morning or on lying or straining, he has no weight loss or behaviour change, and the disc swelling is in one eye with a field defect and RAPD rather than bilateral papilloedema.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner also plays the nurse. Give the observations and glucose when asked, and give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The scalp, jaw and vision symptoms come out only if the candidate asks about them (or asks an open "anything else?" question about the head, eyes or eating). About halfway, the patient says his right eye is getting worse; if acuity is re-checked after this, it is right 6/36. If the candidate orders IV methylprednisolone, ophthalmology or bloods in Part 1, the nurse confirms. Credit these in Part 1 when ordered; in Part 2 credit the candidate who states them or confirms they are running. If the candidate asks for blood results, say they come in Part 2.

In Part 2, read the lead, hand over both results together, then ask the four questions in order. For the fourth, the person playing Fred asks his questions from the Part 2 script.

A high-performing candidate characterises the headache, then asks specifically about scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and vision, screens for PMR and for dangerous causes, and checks for conditions steroids could worsen. They palpate the temporal arteries and examine the eyes properly: acuity, swinging light test, fields and fundoscopy. They recognise visual loss as an emergency, start IV methylprednisolone without waiting for confirmation, and call ophthalmology. In Part 2 they see that worsening vision outweighs a white zone chart. They read the raised ESR and CRP as supportive but not diagnostic, admit under rheumatology, and arrange a biopsy or ultrasound. They counsel Fred honestly about his right eye and the long steroid course.

A borderline candidate takes a generic headache history without the GCA questions, does not palpate the temporal arteries or check acuity, or treats this as migraine. They may wait for the biopsy before steroids, give oral prednisolone despite visual loss, plan discharge with GP follow-up, or give vague safety netting.
explain:
Diagnosis: giant cell arteritis with visual involvement

Giant cell (temporal) arteritis (GCA) is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium arteries that occurs almost only over the age of 50. Incidence rises with age and peaks in the 70s; it is more common in women. The typical picture is a new, often unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness (pain on combing the hair) and jaw claudication: pain and fatigue in the jaw muscles on chewing that builds towards the end of a meal and settles at rest. Jaw claudication is one of the most specific symptoms. Fred has all three, and a blurred right eye.

GCA is urgent because inflammation of the posterior ciliary arteries causes arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy: sudden, usually painless and often permanent visual loss. Fred's findings show the right optic nerve is already ischaemic: reduced acuity, a relative afferent pupillary defect, an inferior field defect, reduced colour vision and a pale ('chalky') swollen disc. Without treatment the other eye can be affected within days. Any visual symptom in suspected GCA needs urgent ophthalmology review and IV pulse corticosteroids.

Polymyalgia rheumatica

About 40 to 50% of people with GCA have polymyalgia rheumatica features: pain and morning stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles and the neck. Always screen for it, and in a patient with PMR ask about headache, jaw and visual symptoms. Fred has no PMR features, which does not argue against GCA.

The headache history: other diagnoses

  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: thunderclap onset, maximal within a minute; Fred's headache came on gradually.
  • Meningitis: fever, neck stiffness, photophobia and rash; none present.
  • Intracranial mass: headache worse in the morning or with lying, coughing or straining, vomiting, weight loss, behaviour change and focal signs; none present.
  • Migraine: throbbing pain with nausea, photophobia, often aura and a past history; a new migraine at 64 is unusual and is a diagnosis of exclusion.
  • Cluster headache: severe orbital pain lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours, with eye watering, nasal congestion and ptosis; not a constant 16-hour ache.
  • Tension-type headache: bilateral, band-like and mild to moderate, without scalp, jaw or visual symptoms.

A new headache over 50 is itself a red flag, and GCA must be considered in every such patient. Acute angle-closure glaucoma also causes headache with a blurred eye, but the eye is red, painful and hard with a mid-dilated pupil, unlike Fred's. The main eye differential is non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, which also gives painless altitudinal field loss with a swollen disc in an older person with vascular risk factors such as hypertension, but the disc is usually hyperaemic rather than pale, and there is no headache, jaw claudication, abnormal temporal artery or markedly raised ESR and CRP.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: every value stays in the white zone while the right eye's acuity falls from 6/18 to 6/36. GCA kills sight rather than disturbing vital signs, so staff concern and the change in vision drive the response. Under Between the Flags, staff concern is itself a Clinical Review criterion.
  • ESR and CRP: both are usually raised. An ESR of 50 mm/h or more is part of the classification criteria. A normal ESR occasionally occurs and does not exclude GCA when the clinical picture fits.
  • Other bloods: thrombocytosis, normocytic anaemia, a raised ALP and a low albumin are common. Thrombocytosis is associated with ischaemic complications. Glucose and renal function are baselines for steroid therapy.

Confirming the diagnosis

Temporal artery biopsy confirms GCA, but its sensitivity is limited because the inflammation is patchy (skip lesions). An adequate length of artery is needed, and a negative biopsy does not exclude GCA. Biopsy findings persist for at least 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start, so steroids must never be delayed for it. Temporal artery ultrasound (a 'halo' sign) is an alternative in experienced centres and is best done within the first week of treatment. The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria require age 50 or more and score sudden visual loss, jaw claudication, new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, an abnormal temporal artery, a raised ESR or CRP, and biopsy or imaging findings. Fred scores well above the threshold before any biopsy. These are classification criteria for research and do not replace clinical judgement.

Management (eTG Rheumatology: giant cell arteritis)

  • Start high-dose corticosteroids as soon as GCA is suspected, before biopsy or imaging.
  • With visual symptoms or visual loss: IV methylprednisolone 500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days, then oral prednisolone (about 1 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg daily). Arrange urgent same-day ophthalmology review.
  • Without visual symptoms: oral prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily.
  • The dose is tapered slowly under rheumatology once symptoms and inflammatory markers settle. Treatment usually lasts a year or more, and relapses are common as the dose falls. Steroid-sparing therapy (for example tocilizumab) is a specialist decision.
  • Admit under rheumatology, with ophthalmology, when vision is involved. Arrange biopsy or ultrasound.
  • Prevent steroid harm: monitor glucose and BP, give calcium and vitamin D and consider a bisphosphonate (glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis), consider gastric protection, and warn about infection, mood and sleep changes.
  • Give simple analgesia. The headache usually improves within days of starting steroids.

Safety netting and follow-up

On the ward, nurses check acuity in both eyes regularly and escalate any visual change, double vision or stroke symptoms immediately. Before discharge, Fred needs to know in plain words to call 000 for any new visual loss in either eye, double vision, or face or limb weakness or speech trouble. He must not stop the steroids suddenly, should carry a steroid card, and should report symptoms of a flare as the dose comes down. Follow-up is with the rheumatology clinic, ophthalmology and the GP, with ESR, CRP, glucose and BP monitoring and a bone density assessment. Visual loss affects fitness to drive under the Austroads vision standards, so he should not drive until his vision has been formally assessed.
points: A new headache in anyone over 50 is giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise. Always ask about scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms and polymyalgia rheumatica.
Jaw claudication is pain or fatigue on chewing that builds towards the end of a meal and settles at rest; it is one of the most specific features of GCA.

Examine the temporal arteries (thickened, tender, reduced pulse) and the eyes properly: acuity in each eye, the swinging light test, fields and fundoscopy. A pale swollen disc with an RAPD means arteritic optic nerve ischaemia.

Start high-dose corticosteroids as soon as GCA is suspected. With any visual symptom, give IV methylprednisolone (500 mg to 1 g daily for 3 days) and get same-day ophthalmology review; never wait for the biopsy.
ESR and CRP are usually raised but can occasionally be normal. Temporal artery biopsy has limited sensitivity (skip lesions) and stays positive for 1 to 2 weeks after steroids start.
Long-term high-dose steroids need glucose and BP monitoring, bone protection, and clear advice never to stop suddenly and to call 000 for any new visual loss.
